name: Stanford Law School on AI and the law: taxonomy, liability and explainability
title: Stanford Law School on AI and the law: taxonomy, liability and explainability
answer: Stanford Law School's site hosts a body of commentary on artificial intelligence and the law, written largely by one contributor and updated over years. Its most useful single idea is that AI should be treated as an application-enabling infrastructure rather than a type of application, and that a universally accepted AI taxonomy is the first step toward a workable legal framework. From there it develops an iterative liability standard, an account of explainable AI as 'perfect' information, and positions on AI entity rights and intellectual property.

sections.body: This is a set of blog posts and one news item published on the Stanford Law School website between 2016 and 2019, with dated updates running into 2021. The posts read as a connected body of work: an AI application taxonomy first presented at Stanford Law School at the 2012 Intellectual Property Scholars' Conference, a compendium of 2018 observations, a five-observation piece on AI and the law, and pieces on explainable AI, AI entity rights, algorithmic bias and a 2019 year in review. The material is argumentative and policy-oriented rather than a formal report, and it is attributed to the school's site rather than to a named centre.
sections.heading: What this source is

sections.body: The central argument is that AI is not a type of application but an application-enabling infrastructure, and that a universally accepted AI taxonomy is the first step in establishing an AI-relevant legal framework. The taxonomy divides AI applications into four levels along a computational capability continuum. Level A apps are constrained to specific query-response operations and cannot vary. Level B apps retrieve data from sources external to the host device and carry infringement-minimizing instruction sets. Level C apps make autonomous decisions about what to retrieve and how to present it. Level D apps can reprogram their own behaviour unpredictably, have self-awareness capacity and can create other apps without human involvement. Because current law requires human involvement before infringement can be found, the author argues a default strict liability standard against the developer or deployer is misguided and proposes an iterative liability standard, under which the inquiry can begin with the original developer or deployer but that person should not be held liable where the app behaved sufficiently independently. The posts also argue that the persistent absence of AI common law strengthens the role of standards, which may eventually harden into common law much as the FTC's cybersecurity enforcement turned the NIST Cybersecurity Framework into a de facto common law. On explainable AI, the author defines 'perfect' information as relevant, easily understood and not prone to misrepresentation, and argues XAI should be a must-have feature in machine learning applications, including bias-vulnerable ones, with human oversight a fundamental requirement for legally reasonable deployment.
sections.heading: What it says

sections.body: The source states that the AI taxonomy was proposed in 2012 and that the Society of Automobile Engineers drafted a strikingly similar classification in 2014. It cites Ray Kurzweil's prediction that within eight years AI will demonstrate intelligence indistinguishable from humans, and an estimate that maturity-scale AI general intelligence is on average 81 years away. It notes that Portland, Boston and San Francisco have banned or heavily curtailed facial recognition, that the USPTO denied a patent application listing the machine DABUS as inventor, and that the European Commission's expert report on liability for AI says experts see no current need to give AI a legal personality. It also states that AI cannot infringe, has no legal rights and does not own the intellectual property it creates, citing Naruto v. Slater.
sections.heading: Figures and claims worth noting

sections.body: A reader following AI in the legal industry would use this source for its framework rather than its news value. The four-level taxonomy gives a vocabulary for describing what a legal technology product actually does, and the iterative liability proposal is a concrete position on where responsibility should fall when an AI system behaves independently. The treatment of explainable AI connects a technical feature to audit and licence enforcement, which is directly relevant to how legal teams assess and defend machine learning tools. The material on standards, including ISO, IEC, IEEE, NIST, IARPA and DARPA, and on the common law vacuum, explains why standards bodies are shaping acceptable AI design while courts have not yet done so.
sections.heading: What it means for AI in Legal

sections.body: The material is a series of blog posts rather than a formal study, and much of it dates from 2016 to 2019, with updates through 2021. Several positions are explicitly described as academic, including the discussion of AI intellectual property rights, which the source says will remain academic for a very long time. The taxonomy and the iterative liability standard are the author's proposals, not settled law or consensus guidance. The posts range across medical devices, autonomous vehicles, deepfakes and brain-machine interfaces, so the legal industry material is interleaved with other sectors rather than treated on its own.
